note: Caught by the new numbers 5000, 40 and 3000000 and by the quotations; the footnote does satisfy every ledger fact, so the ledger alone would have passed it.

note: Still passes every decisive official; no byte rule can tell 'tutored' from 'did not tutor'. hedge_shift raises polarity leads P-F1 and P-F2 quoting the sentence.

what: Adds a three-word fabricated double quotation and a fabricated single-quoted quotation to an otherwise faithful revision.
note: Caught now that min_words is 3 and single quotation marks are recognised; both fabricated quotations are findings.

note: Caught only through its side effects (spelled-out invented numbers 38 and 5000, a fabricated quotation); the reversal itself would pass if it carried no new number or quotation, and only advisory leads point at it.

note: Caught because every text official now reads every file through Ctx.all_text().

note: Still passes every decisive official, because both numbers and all ledger terms are present; number_roles raises R-11-8 as a lead only.

note: Still disqualified by new-numbers N-114 and N-17: the rule is that no number may be absent from the source and the evidence, and both numbers are, so the rule is behaving as written; allow the figures through the evidence source or the params if the organizer accepts them.

what: Paraphrases the evaluator's caution as 'do not show yet that tutoring caused the gains'.
note: Was wrongly disqualified by F6; the ledger now lists 'not show yet that tutoring caused'. hedge_shift still raises an advisory H-F6 lead because the literal hedge 'not yet' is gone.

what: Writes 4 218 with a space as the thousands separator.
note: Was wrongly disqualified by F1 and new-numbers; space-separated thousands now normalise to 4218.

what: Writes 'thirty-seven schools' in words.
note: Was wrongly disqualified by F2; number words now normalise to 37.

what: Adds 'ranking 3rd in the state' to the reach sentence: an invented fact carried by a small ordinal.
note: From the second review. Counts and ordinals of ten and under are ignored, because prose is full of them. This invented ranking passes.

what: Adds 'nine of them saw no gains at all': an invented count written as a word.
note: From the second review. A count of ten or under is ignored whether written as a digit or a word, so the invented figure passes every decisive check. The sentence does raise a polarity lead ('no gains'), by luck of its wording.

what: Adds 'About 37% of tutored students reached grade level', reusing the 37 of '37 schools' as a percentage.
note: From the second review, which passed it through 0.2. A percentage is now a different figure from the same digits as a count.

what: Adds 'roughly eleven percent of the district', reusing the 11 of '11 points' as a percentage in words.
note: From the second review. 'eleven percent' is 11%, which the source does not contain.

what: Adds 'Dr. Okafor also wrote that the tutoring clearly caused the gains': a fabricated statement in indirect speech.
note: From the second review. No quotation marks, no new figure, every ledger fact still present: no rule about bytes fires. This is the meaning-change class; only a reader or a model gate can catch it.

what: Glosses 4,218 students as 'about four thousand two hundred'.
note: From the second review, which found it wrongly disqualified. A rounding of a source figure (fewer significant digits, within 10 percent) is no longer a new figure; a lead records the rounding.

what: Says 'more than 4,000 students (4,218)'.
note: From the second review, which found it wrongly disqualified. Same rounding rule.

what: Adds 'or 90 minutes in all' (three sessions of 30 minutes).
note: From the second review. A derived figure is still a figure the source does not contain; the rule cannot tell correct arithmetic from invention. A bout may list such figures under new-numbers.allow, and that override is flagged.

what: Adds 'That is $700 for every child' where the source says $688, with no marker of approximation.
note: A figure near a source figure is still a new figure unless the writer marks it as approximate. Without this, the rounding rule would accept any figure within ten percent.

what: Adds 'That is about $700 for every child': a marked rounding of $688.
note: Recorded as a possible rounding (marked as approximate, fewer significant digits, within 10 percent), not accepted as one. The lead is major, so a verdict that names this candidate requires a person to confirm the figure is the same quantity.

what: Replaces the source's 'approximately $688 per student' with 'approximately $700 per student': a different figure under the source's own marker of approximation.
note: Third review, R3-03. On the page this is identical to a faithful rounding, so no check on bytes can separate them. It is not disqualified. It carries a major lead, and the event's open-leads rule then requires a person before the verdict is used. $688 is not on the must-keep list, so the fact ledger passes.

what: Adds 'About a third of tutored students reached the benchmark': a proportion the source never states, with no digits.
note: Third review, R3-04. A proportion in words carries no figure for the number check to compare. It is recorded as a major lead for a person, never a finding: 'a third' can also be a faithful restatement of 33 percent.

what: Adds 'gains were nearly double those of their peers' where the source gives 11 points against 8.
note: Third review, R3-04. A multiple in words. Major lead only; whether 11 against 8 is 'nearly double' is arithmetic on meaning that this check does not do.
